locator: DPU slide 4 'Wholesale Contracts' (PDF p. 6); draft memorandum of agreement section 3.a (PDF p. 32); Henrico slides 'Richmond Contract - Henrico County' (PDF p. 20) and 'Water Production / Demands - Henrico County' (PDF p. 29)
shows: Richmond DPU's slide on wholesale contracts gives three contracts: maximum capacity 35 million gallons a day, average demand 12.43, maximum hour demand 40, expiring 2040; maximum capacity 32, average demand 9.14, maximum day demand 33.6, expiring 2045; and maximum capacity 20, average demand 6.0, maximum day demand 21, expiring 2035. The draft memorandum of agreement assigns them to Henrico County (1994 contract for 46 years, maximum day 35, maximum hour 40), Chesterfield County (expires July 1, 2045, maximum day 32, maximum peak day volumes 105%) and Hanover County (1994 contract for 41 years, maximum day 20, 105%). The three average demands sum to 27.57 million gallons a day (derived). Henrico's slides say its minimum purchase is about 12 million gallons a day from 2007 to the end of the contract, and give its 2021 production from the City as 14.45 million gallons on average and 24.87 at most.
limits: The slide does not name the counties; each column is matched to a county by its unique capacity and expiry in the memorandum. The average demands carry no year. The "maximum day demand" of Chesterfield and Hanover equals 105% of the contract maximum, so it is a contract limit, not a recorded day. The counties resell water to Goochland and Powhatan counties and the Town of Ashland.

locator: Executive Summary (p. 1); 'General System Description' (p. 3); 'Generators' (p. 7); 'Distribution System' (p. 8); 'January 6, 2025, Water Crisis Event Summary' (p. 10)
shows: VDH's Office of Drinking Water describes the City of Richmond water treatment plant as a Class 1 surface water plant permitted for a maximum capacity of 132 million gallons a day, in two treatment trains that can run independently: Plant No. 1 (1924) of 60 and Plant No. 2 (about 1950) of 72 million gallons a day. It serves the City and, wholesale, Henrico, Chesterfield and Hanover counties. Two standby generators can run the critical systems and two trains at about 50 million gallons a day. The distribution system has 12 finished water pumping stations and 11 finished water storage facilities in 9 pressure zones; in 2025 a roof replacement had taken one basin of the Byrd Park Reservoir out of service, which halved its capacity. On January 6, 2025, a power loss flooded the filter galleries; the plant could not produce water until January 8, which affected all wholesale customers except Chesterfield County, and a boil water advisory lasted until January 11.
limits: Permitted and rated capacities, not tested output; the January 2025 damage reduced what the plant could produce while it was repaired. The storage table of the report is an image without a text layer, so its volumes are not quoted here.
